When I started working as an analyst for a basketball team, the coach gave me one rule. Never show me a number without the line behind it. Over the last twenty years, three-point attempts in professional basketball have more than doubled. On its own, that number tells you almost nothing. The line tells you the story. Our own attempts rose steadily for four seasons, reached a peak, and then leveled off. At the same time, our shooting percentage dropped slightly. So the coach asked a better question. Are we shooting more because we are better, or only because everybody else is? The data could not answer that. What it did was make the question sharper, and that is roughly what good data always does.

Most people describe a graph from left to right, one number at a time, and by the third number the listener is lost. Try three steps instead. First, the big picture. Overall, the number of applicants has risen over the last ten years. Second, the biggest change. There was a sharp drop in one year, followed by a steady recovery. Third, one detail that surprised you. And please round your numbers. Nobody remembers forty-seven point three percent. Everybody remembers just under half. Finally, watch two small words. Prices rose by ten percent tells me the difference. Prices rose to ten dollars tells me where they ended. Mix them up, and your listener gets the wrong story from the right numbers.
